video_title: Building a big, abundant, clean grid
gist: Clean-energy policy analyst Jane Flegel tells Volts host David Roberts that US electricity demand growth from the data-center buildout is a once-in-a-generation chance to finance a much larger clean grid, and that the binding constraint is now federal permitting and the total absence of grid planning rather than technology cost. She argues the risks of underbuilding dwarf the risks of overbuilding, warns that behind-the-meter gas could supply more than half of new US data-center capacity by 2028 with roughly 100% gas emissions rates, and pushes for a federal or state fund capitalized by hyperscalers plus a federal permitting deal covering NEPA, the Clean Water Act and interregional transmission siting.

insights.claim: Jane Flegel argues carbon pricing cannot work as the primary climate lever because carbon, unlike HFCs or conventional pollutants, is embedded throughout the entire economy rather than concentrated in a few producers and geographies with ready substitutes.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Investors should discount scenarios where a US carbon price re-emerges as the central decarbonization mechanism and instead underwrite subsidy-, procurement- and permitting-driven policy regimes.
insights.quote: Carbon unlike these other pollutants is embedded deeply kind of everywhere in the economy.

insights.claim: The 'green spiral' theory Flegel works from holds that government investment drives clean-tech costs down, deployment creates industries and jobs, and those industries then become a political constituency powerful enough to demand more climate policy.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Policy durability tracks industry scale and lobbying capacity, so sectors with large installed bases and employment footprints are the better bets for surviving hostile administrations.

insights.claim: Flegel cites roughly 90% cost declines for solar and for batteries and about 70% for wind as evidence the cost-decline leg of the green spiral worked, while the political-power leg largely failed.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Cheap hardware is no longer the differentiator; political and permitting execution is where returns now diverge across clean-energy assets.
insights.quote: we have 90% cost declines for solar and batteries and incredible same for batteries, 70% for wind

insights.claim: Flegel says climate advocates cannot defeat entrenched fossil interests with 'a coalition of the marginalized' and must instead recruit part of capital onto their side, the way the New Deal did.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Signals that clean-energy trade groups and hyperscalers, not environmental NGOs, are the coalition partners whose lobbying spend will determine future US energy policy.
insights.quote: you are not going to roll them with like a coalition of the marginalized. It's the same way that the New Deal worked. You got to have some part of capital on your side.

insights.claim: Flegel says the vast majority of the IRA remains intact after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and that the law still puts the US on a materially better emissions trajectory than the counterfactual.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Frames the 'glass half full' side of the post-OBBBA modeling fight and implies IRA-dependent project pipelines are less impaired than headline coverage suggests.
insights.quote: look I mean the vast majority of that law remains intact

insights.claim: Flegel dismisses the dueling post-OBBBA models as both fake and internally inconsistent because each is answering a different question, and says the fight became heated mainly because Lily Bermel's normative takeaway was that advocates should not spend political capital reinstating solar and wind tax credits.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Warns against treating competing decarbonization model outputs as investable signal; the underlying political question is whether solar and wind credits get fought for at all.
insights.quote: part of the problems with these models is that a they're fake and b they're like they are all asking different questions

insights.claim: Flegel argues the 'find the tons' accounting used to build the US nationally determined contribution biased the IRA toward near-term tonnage like incremental commercial solar subsidies and away from clean steel, clean chemicals and clean cement, whose payoff shows up only through long, unmodelable global innovation chains.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Industrial decarbonization technologies remain structurally underfunded by US policy relative to their emissions importance, which is both a gap and a potential opportunity if policy reframes.
insights.quote: these find the tons exercises bias you toward near-term large tons

insights.claim: Flegel says buy-clean and other demand-side industrial tools failed because there were no genuinely cleaner goods on the market to purchase, so the incentives collapsed into a version of Buy American rather than pulling novel clean technologies into commercialization.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Demand-side green procurement mandates should not be underwritten as a reliable revenue pull for first-of-a-kind industrial plants without matching supply-side capital.
insights.quote: I kept arguing like we don't have cleaner goods to buy.

insights.claim: Flegel describes an epistemic crisis in the environmental NGO world where for a period one could not call climate change a risk-management challenge without being labeled a climate denier, destroying the capacity for balanced trade-off analysis that policymakers need.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Signals that advocacy-sourced analysis should be discounted as an input to energy forecasting, and that there is an unmet market for genuinely neutral energy policy analysis.

insights.claim: Flegel says the environmental movement's institutional DNA was built to stop bad things under a pollution-control paradigm, and is poorly suited to the current era where states have already legislated clean-energy targets and now actually have to build to meet them.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A capability gap between legislated state targets and actual buildout is where policy failure and investment opportunity will both show up over the next several years.
insights.quote: turns out you got actually meet those targets

insights.claim: Flegel argues the abundance movement is wrong to under-emphasize state capacity while the pro-public-investment left is wrong to propose large direct public infrastructure investment while insisting NEPA needs no reform.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Any credible large-scale public infrastructure program is permitting-constrained, so NEPA reform is a prerequisite for public-power and public-financing agendas alike, not just private ones.
insights.quote: it actually is the case that if you want to have very large public infrastructure projects, you need to grapple in a serious way with the permanent constraints

insights.claim: Flegel says the belief that a decisive bloc of climate voters existed drove the Biden White House's climate prioritization, and that belief has been deflated by the most recent election.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Removes a key assumption underpinning expectations of aggressive future Democratic climate legislation and argues for lower policy-beta in climate-dependent positions.
insights.quote: there was a belief which I think proved to be false unfortunately that there were a bunch of climate voters

themes.theme: Data center bargain and grid funds

insights.claim: Flegel proposes an American Grid Infrastructure Fund in which hyperscalers pay into a dedicated fund in exchange for social license to build, capturing generational data-center wealth for grid investment rather than leaving it to opaque rate cases.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A new policy instrument to watch: if adopted, it converts hyperscaler capex into a per-project charge that materially changes data-center siting economics.

insights.claim: Flegel argues large-load tariffs are necessary but insufficient because they were never designed to handle the scale of the data-center buildout and cannot resolve regional and interregional transmission cost allocation, which she calls a nightmare.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Expect the data-center cost fight to escalate past state tariff proceedings into federal transmission cost-allocation battles, a major source of regulatory risk for interregional lines.

insights.claim: Flegel says state-vs-state cost allocation fights are already toxic, with Virginia having blamed Maryland's clean energy laws for transmission upgrade costs and Maryland now blaming Virginia's data-center policy for the same.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Interstate cost-allocation litigation in PJM is a concrete near-term risk to transmission project timelines and to data-center siting in Virginia.

insights.claim: Flegel reports fund variants are already spreading beyond her federal proposal: Sam Ricketts published a state-level version, New York's Hochul flagged a fund when announcing a pause, and Virginia has enacted a charge on data-center electricity consumption that flows into the general fund.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: State-level data-center levies are proliferating fast, raising the effective cost of new US data-center capacity and favoring jurisdictions that move last.

insights.claim: Flegel and Roberts agree the anti-data-center backlash has become a vessel for generalized anxiety about inequality and loss of control, so it cannot be defused by technocratic answers like large-load tariffs that nobody understands.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk to data-center siting is political rather than analytic, so utility-commission wins will not translate into permission to build.
insights.quote: There is a part of it that like feels a little like mass hysteria driven.

insights.claim: Flegel says hyperscalers' failure to buy community goodwill with cheap co-benefits is driven less by malice than by competitive dynamics — a firm that slows down to add community investments loses the compute race to a rival rolling in jet-engine-derived gas turbines.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Voluntary industry standards on data-center siting will not emerge without coordination or regulation, since defection is individually rational.

insights.claim: Flegel cites SemiAnalysis estimating that behind-the-meter power could account for more than half of new US data-center capacity by 2028, driven not by preference but because grid headroom is running out in the most congested places and interconnection is too slow.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A concrete, datable forecast: if it holds, gas turbine and distributed generation suppliers capture a majority of new data-center load through 2028.
insights.quote: semi analysis is saying that behind the meter could account for more than half of new US data center capacity by 2028

insights.claim: Flegel identifies keeping data centers on the grid rather than behind the meter as the single biggest decarbonization risk facing the US power sector.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Frames grid-connection policy, not generation subsidies, as the highest-leverage emissions variable in the AI buildout.
insights.quote: We got to get them on the grid, man.

insights.claim: Flegel's first mechanism against behind-the-meter gas is resource-mix dilution: a grid-connected data center draws a blended emissions rate including zero-marginal-cost renewables, nuclear and hydro plus efficient combined cycle, whereas an off-grid facility runs at effectively 100% gas.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Quantifies why grid-connected load is strategically preferable for emissions and why off-grid data centers face the greatest future carbon-policy exposure.
insights.quote: the effective emissions rate of that facility is the blended rate

insights.claim: Flegel's second mechanism is that off-grid data-center generation is optimized for speed rather than thermal efficiency, producing simple-cycle and aeroderivative turbines running near 100% capacity factor that are arguably worse than coal, plus diesel and kerosene backup.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Off-grid AI power is materially dirtier per MWh than assumed in most load-growth emissions models, a downside risk to utility and corporate emissions disclosures.
insights.quote: you end up with these crazy inefficient like arguably worse than coal gas plants

insights.claim: Flegel rejects the assumption that behind-the-meter data centers will eventually connect to the grid, arguing that a firm which built a 400 MW gas plant and then waits seven years for interconnection would rationally use the interconnection to double the data center rather than retire the gas.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter gas assets built now should be modeled as permanent additions to the generation stack, not as bridge capacity that retires on interconnection.
insights.quote: if you built a 400 megawatt gas plant to power your data center facility and then like in seven years you get interconnection why wouldn't you just like double the size of your data center

insights.claim: Flegel points to Tyler Norris's non-firm interconnection proposal — data centers accepting partial curtailment at defined times in exchange for far faster grid connection — as the most promising near-term tool, noting FERC is pushing it and some RTOs are working on it.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Flexible-load interconnection is the regulatory reform most likely to unlock grid-connected data-center capacity quickly, favoring operators with curtailable workloads.

insights.claim: Flegel observes that the states where data-center development has pushed rates down are mostly states that already had a lot of spare capacity built in advance of demand.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A screenable heuristic: states with existing generation and transmission headroom can absorb data-center load without ratepayer backlash, making them the durable siting winners.
insights.quote: it has mostly been in states that had like a lot of spare capacity

insights.claim: Flegel takes an explicitly pro-overbuilding position, arguing the risks of underbuilding the grid are far larger than the risks of overbuilding as long as ratepayers are not the ones bearing the overbuild risk.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Directly opposes the prevailing affordability-politics push to invest less, and implies sustained upside for transmission and generation capex if her framing wins.
insights.quote: I think the risks of underbuilding are way bigger than the risks of overbuilding.

insights.claim: Flegel cites Texas's CREZ transmission buildout as the model for building in advance of demand, noting it let large volumes of low-cost clean energy connect quickly and enabled demand growth including oil and gas load.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: The concrete US precedent for anticipatory transmission investment, and the template states will cite when justifying proactive builds.
insights.quote: Notably Texas did this with their transmission when they did cres

insights.claim: Flegel defends clean firm capacity on risk-management rather than cost grounds, arguing that the transmission-plus-storage path has its own severe siting, permitting and financing failure modes and that a diversified system with different failure modes is genuinely better.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Reframes clean firm investment as insurance against permitting failure, which supports geothermal and nuclear allocations even if storage costs keep falling.

insights.claim: Flegel argues that if transmission expansion stays blocked while demand growth continues, meeting that demand cleanly would have to happen through clean firm behind the meter, because the physical footprint and redundancy needed for solar-plus-battery-only data centers is impractical.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Makes behind-the-meter advanced nuclear and geothermal the contingent winner if federal permitting reform fails, a direct hedge against transmission policy risk.
insights.quote: the physical footprint of powering these data centers with like solar and batteries alone is just like very difficult to imagine

insights.claim: Flegel says no one is structurally in charge of planning the grid in most of the country, with FERC Order 1920 pushing RTOs toward 20-year transmission planning but barely taking effect and nothing comparable existing on the generation side.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Order 1920 is the only planning backstop in place and is not yet binding, so near-term transmission expansion still depends on ad hoc state and utility action.
insights.quote: nobody is structurally in most of this country in charge of planning anything on the grid

insights.claim: Flegel breaks utility incentive problems into four distinct issues that are usually bundled together: utility political influence, the incentive to overbuild, the incentive to build the wrong stuff, and the cost of capital.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A cleaner diagnostic than the generic 'utilities are incentivized to overbuild' argument, and it points to different remedies with very different capex consequences.

insights.claim: Flegel argues suppressing utility return on equity is a blunt instrument that discourages capex generally rather than only the unwanted capex, and is not even solving the right problem in a moment when underbuilding is the larger risk.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the most popular current utility-reform proposal; if regulators follow it, ROE compression would suppress exactly the grid investment the demand boom requires.
insights.quote: this slam down roe, it just feels to me like a pretty blunt instrument that discourages capex more generally, not just the capex you don't want

insights.claim: Flegel says performance-based ratemaking has a genuinely mixed empirical track record in Massachusetts, Hawaii and the UK, apparently because defining the outcomes that matter is very hard, so it should not be treated as a panacea.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence undercuts a reform widely assumed to be the fix for utility misalignment, tempering expectations for PBR-driven utility business model change.
insights.quote: it is like not been clearly vindicated by the results

insights.claim: Flegel's preferred affordability lever is capital structure rather than allowed returns: push utilities to finance more capex with debt instead of equity, via securitization, DOE Loan Programs Office funding or similar tools.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A concrete, underdiscussed lever: more debt financing lowers revenue requirements without killing capex, and she notes the Trump administration effectively granted Southern Company money for this purpose.
insights.quote: the issue is the cost of capital, which is about capital structure, not return on equity

insights.claim: Flegel supports getting general-public-benefit programs off electricity bills and onto the general tax base, citing an LBNL report showing grid hardening and wildfire mitigation costs are a non-trivial share of bills in many states.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Cost-shifting from ratepayers to taxpayers is emerging as the third option in the affordability debate, and California wildfire cost recovery is where it plays out first.
insights.quote: A third option is like change who's paying for stuff.

insights.claim: Flegel cites standard energy burden literature showing low-income households spend 8 to 17% of income on energy versus 2 to 3% for higher-income households, making the rate base the most regressive way to fund public programs.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: The quantitative basis for the political durability of the affordability backlash and for shifting costs off bills as electrification expands.
insights.quote: low-income households spend 8 to 17% of their income on energy where it's like 2 to 3% for higher inome households

insights.claim: Flegel argues permitting reform asymmetrically advantages clean energy because solar and wind require roughly 20 and 200 times respectively the permitted land area of gas per unit of energy delivered, and transmission rights of way run two to three times wider than a comparable gas pipeline.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: The strongest quantitative rebuttal to the claim that permitting reform mainly helps fossil fuels; more dispersed, linear infrastructure carries categorically more permitting exposure.
insights.quote: solar and wind require roughly 20 and 200 times respectively the permitted land area of gas per unit of energy delivered

insights.claim: Flegel cites federal land avoidance as the overlooked NEPA dynamic: federal lands are 21% of the lower 48 but host only 3% of US onshore wind, solar and geothermal capacity, despite the disproportionately federal desert southwest having the country's best solar and geothermal resources.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Quantifies a massive untapped resource base gated purely by federal permitting friction, and identifies the specific unlock that would make desert southwest resources developable.
insights.quote: federal lands are 21% of the lower 48, but they host only 3% of US onshore wind, solar, and geothermal capacity

insights.claim: Flegel reports developer survey results showing over 85% of transmission developers and over 65% of solar developers rate federal permitting more onerous than state or local, and that 82% of developers surveyed this year said they had intentionally sited a project to avoid triggering federal permitting.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Direct revealed-preference evidence that federal permitting is distorting siting decisions today, meaning reform would reallocate where projects get built, not just how fast.
insights.quote: 82% of developers surveyed this year said they'd intentionally cited a project to avoid triggering federal permitting

insights.claim: Flegel ranks the severity of clean-energy build barriers as federal permitting first, state and local permitting second, and interconnection third, arguing interconnection problems are largely downstream of insufficient transmission capacity rather than a standalone process failure.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Reorders the standard priority list, implying that queue reform alone will not unlock the pipeline without new transmission capacity.
insights.quote: I think federal permitting is like really the top followed by state and local followed by interconnection

insights.claim: Flegel warns NEPA exposure for transmission is rising sharply: only 3 to 12% of new transmission lines required a full environmental impact statement over the last decade, but 26% of new line miles did in 2024, and roughly half of the 26,000-plus miles now planned are expected to trigger an EIS as building shifts west onto federal lands.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Historical NEPA rates badly understate future transmission permitting risk, so project timelines for planned western interregional lines should be extended substantially absent reform.
insights.quote: of the 26,000 plus miles of transmission now planned an estimated half of it are likely to trigger an EPA

insights.claim: Flegel reports that 17% of continental US county land mass now heavily restricts wind and/or solar, roughly double the share of only a few years ago.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Local siting restrictions are compounding fast and shrinking the developable land base, a structural headwind to onshore renewables independent of federal policy.
insights.quote: 17% of the continental US county land mass now heavily restricts wind and or solar, which is double the share only a few years ago

insights.claim: Flegel says the most important and most likely NEPA change is litigation reform to judicial remedies, specifically time-limited review, because the current default lets courts hold a project up indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Remedies reform, not agency deadlines, is the provision to watch in any permitting bill, since it directly caps tail risk on project timelines.
insights.quote: courts can just like hold up a project indefinitely and like we should just have time limited review

insights.claim: Flegel argues permitting reform must be passed now rather than after the election, because the reforms take years to work through agencies and courts, a 2029 Democratic administration would want to hit the ground running, and she is highly suspicious that passage gets easier post-election.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Argues the legislative window is now, so the probability of a federal permitting deal is higher in this session than in the next — a timing call for transmission-exposed assets.
insights.quote: I'm highly suspicious that after the election, it will be easier to pass this bill

insights.claim: Flegel identifies a rare political opening on federal transmission planning and permitting because utilities and states, the historic blockers, currently have much less power with both parties than they have historically had.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: The affordability and data-center backlash has weakened utility lobbying leverage, creating a narrow window for federal transmission siting authority that would be highly valuable to interregional line developers.
insights.quote: this is one of very few moments where you might be able to roll them on federal transmission planning and permitting

insights.claim: Flegel says hyperscalers are in fact pushing for federal permitting reform, but quietly, and that Republicans would likely not be at the negotiating table without that constituency's pressure.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Big tech is the hidden sponsor of the federal permitting negotiation, meaning the bill's fate is tied to AI capex sentiment rather than to climate politics.
insights.quote: Look, I think many of them are. It's just been a very quiet negotiation is the honest answer.

insights.claim: Flegel argues efforts to win Republicans on climate fail because advocates never specify the ask, and that concrete asks like defending nuclear tax credits or embedding CO2 emissions in trade policy are winnable while grandiose emissions targets are not.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Maps where bipartisan durability actually exists: nuclear and trade-linked carbon measures are far more defensible than solar and wind credits or economy-wide targets.

insights.claim: Flegel says she was badly wrong in expecting climate to become a normal policy issue with competing partisan solution sets, and that the degree of cultural backlash specifically against solar and wind has freaked her out.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Technology-level partisan polarization means solar and wind carry a permanent political risk premium in the US that nuclear and geothermal do not.
insights.quote: the way the technology polarization has played out has freaked me out a bunch

insights.claim: Flegel says the clean-energy industry needs to directly fund Republicans to advocate for its interests, and that accountability tactics like the solar PAC primarying obstructive Republicans must be paired with cultivating champions, which remains underattended.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Clean-energy political spending is shifting from NGO-led advocacy to industry-funded electoral pressure, a leading indicator of the sector's policy durability.
insights.quote: I really think the industry needs to like give Republicans money to advocate for their stuff.

insights.claim: Flegel warns that fiscal room in 2029 will be severely constrained, citing Brendan Duke at CBPP tracking the cost of undoing SNAP and Medicaid cuts alone, which forces ruthless prioritization of a few clean-grid priorities.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: A future Democratic administration will have little fiscal space for a second IRA, so the next climate agenda is likely to be regulatory and permitting-based rather than subsidy-based.

insights.claim: Flegel argues consensus-based coalitional politics inside the Democratic party suppresses creative policy because 70-year-old organizations dependent on specific funders cannot go on record for ideas like public power, so she is instead canvassing the 30 smartest people she knows to build a federal agenda.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: The next federal climate agenda is being drafted outside the established NGO coalition, so watching individual analysts rather than institutions is the better early signal.
insights.quote: identify the 30 smartest people I know on like the topics I think matter and been like tell me what you think we should do

insights.claim: Flegel identifies the climate donor class as the least transparent and most influential constraint on elected officials, pressuring them through and via the advocacy groups with concerns sometimes out of touch with the electorate.
insights.speaker: Jane Flegel
insights.so_what: Public factional fights over climate policy are often downstream of opaque donor decisions, so funder behavior is a leading indicator of which policies get pushed.
insights.quote: you have a very large donor class that is itself putting pressure on electeds
